correctness.rationale: For u=x^p-y^q, small negative y gives u>=|y|^q>|y|^r, so the negative region occurs only at positive y. On |u|<y^r both inverse x roots exist, and their combined Jacobian is comparable to y^{-gamma}, gamma=q(1-1/p). With u=y^r v the negative integral has y power r(1-2s)-gamma; the v integral is finite for s<1 and the y integral diverges at equality r(1-2s)-gamma=-1. This gives beta<1/2; higher s then diverge by monotonicity. The negative-y wedge |x|<=|y|^(q/p) has f comparable to |y|^(2q) and proves divergence on the positive side at alpha=(1/p+1/q)/2. For s<alpha, the positive portion of |u|<2y^r uses the same y exponent as the negative strip, plus only simple v=+/-1 poles, and converges since alpha<beta. The complement is dominated by |x^p-y^q|^(-2s): in the near-cusp region scaling x=|y|^(q/p)v gives y power q/p-2qs and at most simple v poles, while the x-dominant region gives x power p/q-2ps. All exponents pass exactly as needed. The two factors have primitive parametrizations y=t^p, x=t^q times units, with first coprime exponent q; the factor ideal equals (x^p-y^q,y^r), of colength pr. The beta formula is strictly increasing and invertible for r with fixed p,q.
